podcast_name: Resourceful Designer: Strategies for running a graphic design business
episode_title: Stop Selling the Blueprint. Start Selling the House - RD367
question: What is the difference between selling the blueprint and selling the house in design client pitches?
transcript_excerpt: The blueprint is the process and deliverables you explain—file formats, revision rounds, discovery questionnaires, and technical details. The house is what the client actually wants: the result and change in their business. For example, a landscaping company client doesn't want a logo; they want people to remember their name when they see their trucks and to be able to raise prices without apologizing. As a designer, you must stop talking about your process long enough to find out what the house looks like in the client's mind, then describe it so clearly they can picture walking through that front door.

podcast_name: Resourceful Designer: Strategies for running a graphic design business
episode_title: Stop Selling the Blueprint. Start Selling the House - RD367
question: How should designers position their discovery calls when working with larger corporate clients versus small business owners?
transcript_excerpt: With larger corporate clients, the person you're talking to—like a marketing coordinator or communications manager—must justify spending money to their boss or board. Their house isn't a beautiful brand; it's 'Can I defend this decision and make me look good?' Stop walking them through your process step-by-step. Instead, ask: Who else needs to approve this? What will they want to know? Six months after launch, what would make you look back and say this was a great decision? Help them walk into that meeting holding something they can point to and give them language to sell it internally.

podcast_name: Resourceful Designer: Strategies for running a graphic design business
episode_title: Stop Selling the Blueprint. Start Selling the House - RD367
question: What are examples of house talk versus blueprint talk when pitching a logo or branding project?
transcript_excerpt: Blueprint talk: 'I'll provide three initial concepts, two rounds of revisions, and final files in all standard formats, plus a one-page brand guide.' House talk: 'Right now you feel like your trucks and yard signs look like every other landscaper in town. When we're done, people are gonna see your trucks parked in a neighbor's driveway and remember your name. You'll be able to raise your prices without feeling like you have to apologize for it because your brand will finally look like the quality of the work that you do.' The supporting details still matter, but they should come after you've described the outcome.

podcast_name: Resourceful Designer: Strategies for running a graphic design business
episode_title: Stop Selling the Blueprint. Start Selling the House - RD367
question: What practical sentence should designers complete before writing a proposal to identify the house?
transcript_excerpt: Complete this sentence out loud: 'When this is done, you'll finally be able to...' Whatever comes after those words is the house. Examples: 'When this is done, you'll finally be able to hand out your business card with pride.' Or 'When this is done, you'll finally be able to stop answering the same five questions by email every day.' Or 'When this is done, you'll finally be able to show the partners exactly how many leads the new website brought in.' The word 'finally' acknowledges that your client has been waiting, that there's been frustration or a gap. If you can't finish that sentence, you're not ready to pitch yet—go back and ask more questions.

podcast_name: Resourceful Designer: Strategies for running a graphic design business
episode_title: Stop Selling the Blueprint. Start Selling the House - RD367
question: What kinds of discovery questions should designers ask to uncover the house instead of just the blueprint?
transcript_excerpt: House questions go deeper than 'What colors do you like?' or 'How many pages do you need?' Instead ask: 'Why now? What made you decide this was the time to reach out?' Or 'If this project turns out perfectly, what's different about your business a year from now?' Or 'What's frustrating you most about how things are right now?' Or 'When you imagine showing this off for the first time, who are you showing it to?' That last question often reveals the real house—sometimes they want to show it to customers, sometimes to investors, and sometimes quietly to their parents, a former boss, or a former mentor they want to prove something to. Stay curious longer than feels comfortable; the real house is usually two or three questions deep.
